issues.legal_issue: A state government may make an ancillary rule providing a speedy recovery mechanism to carry out the objectives of the parent enactment.
material_facts: The State Government framed a rule under its general power to make rules to carry out the parent enactment.
The enactment seeks to promote and protect micro, small and medium enterprises.
The rule allows sums awarded in disputes under the enactment to be recovered through a speedier mechanism.
The recovery rule implements the enactment’s recovery objective without changing its scope or policy.
issues.conclusion: The recovery rule was within the State Government’s rule-making authority and was a valid ancillary measure.
issues.legal_principle: A general power to make rules to carry out an Act permits rules that are ancillary to and implement the Act’s purposes, but not rules that enlarge or alter its scope or policy. The Court applied the principles in Agricultural Market Committee v. Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd. (1997) 5 SCC 516, Dr. Mahachandra Prasad Singh v. Chairman, Bihar Legislative Council (2004) 8 SCC 747, and Academy of Nutrition Improvement v. Union of India (2011) 8 SCC 274.

rule.if: subordinate_rule_challenge and broad_rulemaking_power and recovery_rule_advances_parent_act_object and recovery_rule_is_ancillary

predicates.subordinate_rule_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a rule made under a parent enactment.
predicates.broad_rulemaking_power: The parent enactment gives the rule-maker a general power to make rules to carry out its provisions.
predicates.recovery_rule_advances_parent_act_object: The rule provides a recovery mechanism that advances an objective of the parent enactment.
predicates.recovery_rule_is_ancillary: The rule implements the parent enactment’s policy without enlarging or changing its scope.

issues.definition: When a challenged rule is made under a broad rule-making power and provides an ancillary mechanism advancing the parent enactment’s objective, the rule is within the rule-maker’s authority.

issues.legal_issue: Providing an alternative method of recovering an arbitral award does not invalidate an existing civil-court execution method merely because the methods differ.
material_facts: An arbitral award could be enforced as a court decree through civil-court execution.
The challenged rule also permitted recovery of the awarded sum through a different procedure.
Both procedures were intended to recover the awarded amount, and the award-holder could elect which remedy to pursue.
issues.conclusion: The alternative recovery procedure was not repugnant to the civil-court execution procedure; the award-holder could choose between the available remedies.
issues.legal_principle: Plural remedies may remain available even if their procedures are inconsistent, and the person entitled to recover may elect one of them. The Court relied on Bihar State Co-operative Marketing Union Ltd. v. Uma Shankar Sharan (1992) 4 SCC 196 and applied harmonious construction, noting that the principle that a specific provision excludes a general one does not invalidate provisions that provide different remedies.

predicates.arbitral_award_enforcement_case: The proceeding concerns enforcement of an arbitral award.
predicates.civil_execution_remedy_exists: The award can be enforced through execution in a civil court as if it were a decree.
predicates.alternative_recovery_remedy_exists: A separate procedure is also available to recover the amount awarded.

issues.definition: When an arbitral award can be enforced through civil-court execution and an alternative recovery procedure is available, the award-holder may choose either remedy.

issues.legal_issue: A speedy recovery procedure for an adjudicated award is not arbitrary or discriminatory merely because it differs from ordinary civil-court execution.
material_facts: The recovery procedure applied after the dispute had been adjudicated and an award had been made.
The award had not been challenged within the applicable period for seeking to set it aside.
The procedure was intended to secure speedy recovery for micro, small and medium enterprises.
The Court found the procedure reasonable and found that it deprived the debtor of no substantial or valuable privilege.
issues.conclusion: The recovery procedure was not illegal, arbitrary, harsh or discriminatory under Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Legislation is presumed constitutional, with attention to whether affected persons receive a fair deal; public interest and the need for effective, speedy recovery may justify a recovery mechanism that operates without ordinary civil-court execution. A procedural difference is not discriminatory merely because another procedure provides different safeguards, where the procedure is reasonable and does not deprive a person of a substantial or valuable privilege. The Court relied on Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India (2004) 4 SCC 311 and distinguished, among others, Suraj Mall Mohta & Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri (1955) 1 SCR 448, Shree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri AIR 1955 SC 13, and Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay (1974) 2 SCC 402.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and recovery_follows_adjudication and award_not_set_aside_within_challenge_period and procedure_is_reasonable and no_substantial_privilege_is_denied

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenges a recovery procedure as arbitrary or discriminatory.
predicates.recovery_follows_adjudication: The recovery procedure is used after the underlying dispute has been adjudicated and an award has been made.
predicates.award_not_set_aside_within_challenge_per: The award has not been set aside through a challenge brought within the applicable period.
predicates.procedure_is_reasonable: The recovery procedure is reasonable in its operation.
predicates.no_substantial_privilege_is_denied: The procedure does not deprive the debtor of a substantial or valuable privilege.

issues.definition: A challenged recovery procedure is not arbitrary or discriminatory when it follows adjudication, the award has not been set aside within the applicable challenge period, the procedure is reasonable, and no substantial privilege is denied.
